thread.title: 2 Cash-Rich Stocks To Buy Before They Jump Higher

author: Richard Saintvilus
title: 2 Cash-Rich Stocks To Buy Before They Jump Higher
text:
Shutterstock photo There’s a saying on Wall Street, "companies can fake earnings, but they can't fake cash." I don’t know who coined that phrase, but whoever first said it had a basic understanding that cash is arguably the strongest (and often the surest) way not only to measure a company's financial health, but also its operational strength.
One of the most popular metrics investors use to evaluate stock prices is the price to earnings ratio. But if we agree that companies can “fake” earnings, as the Quote: suggests, this metric can be gamed. Savvy investors, by contrast, often consider the price-to-free-cash-flow (PFCF) metric to be a far superior equivalent. Not only can the PFCF be compared to peer companies, it’s also useful against a key benchmark such as the S&P 500.
As the name suggests, “cash flow” measures of the amount of cash flowing through a business, while excluding arbitrary metrics and other intangible items such as depreciation and amortization. Meanwhile, free cash flow, which refers to the amount of cash flowing into a business, excludes the cost a business incurs — known as “maintenance capital expenditures” — needed to make to keep operations in good order.
It’s helpful to know that the S&P 500 median PFCF ratio six months ago stood at 34.66. Since the recent stock market correction, that number has fallen to 30.97. The lower the number, the more attractive the equity is perceived to be. Thus, in an unpredictable and volatile stock market, long-term investors looking for dependability and reliability should consider cash-rich companies — those that have strong free cash flows that are growing. And if those companies pay a dividend, it’s an added bonus. Here are two stocks long term investors should consider.
Micron ( MU ) - $33.74, PFCF = 4.23
The nation’s largest memory manufacturer, which has been one of the best-performing technology stocks in the past two years, took a pounding in the last half of 2018. In recent years, Micron has benefited from strong demand for its memory chips — the type that store information in mobile devices and help processors crunch data in computers and data centers. Its chips are used in electronic devices from the likes of Apple ( AAPL ), Intel ( INTC ) and HP ( HPQ ), among others. But there is now fear its growth has peaked.
Micron stock reached its 52-week high of $64 last summer, but has since plunged more than 50%. The stock closed Tuesday at $33.74 and it’s still down some 40% from its high. Analysts still recommend the shares with a Buy rating with a consensus price target of $47, suggesting 40% premium from current levels. Micron should be on the radar of investors who are looking for a strong turnaround candidate for 2019.
Mylan ( MYL ) - $29.87, PFCF = 7.90
Pharmaceutical specialist Mylan, maker of the EpiPen, struggled in 2018 due to a combination of factors, including various operational setbacks, causing lackluster earnings results. Mylan also took a hit to its top line with the Food and Drug Administration, last August, green-lighted rival Teva Pharmaceuticals ( TEVA ) to market a generic competitor to the EpiPen. As we enter 2019, Mylan shares, currently priced at $29.87, are trading some 37% below their 52-week high of $47.82. From my vantage point, it’s a solid time to buy.
The company last quarter delivered earnings results that showed a strong 14% jump year over year, suggesting it is not too far off from regaining its health. In November, David Maris, analyst at Wells Fargo upgraded the shares to Outperform, saying he believes the risks are fully priced into the stock. Maris is not alone. Mylan still has a consensus Buy rating and 12-month price target of $45, suggesting a 50% premium from current levels.
